name: Third-party SDK data sharing
plain: Any SDK in an app can read what the app can read and send it to its own servers.
meaning: Third-party code inherits all of the app's permissions, so one SDK can collect location or IDs for a data broker. Stores respond with manifests, disclosure rules and bans.

android.store_policy: Play: you are responsible for SDK behavior; Play SDK Index; Data safety must include SDK collection; 2020 to 2022 bans of data-selling SDKs

ios.store_policy: Privacy manifests, SDK signatures for listed SDKs, App Review 5.1.2
ios.note: Apple's privacy report in Xcode aggregates manifests; Dec 2020 Apple and Google both removed the X-Mode location SDK.

data.metric: Whatever the host app can access

limits.headline: Can share anything the app can see with its add on tools, who send it on
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens whenever the app runs
can: Collect location, IDs and other data the app has been allowed
Send what it collects to its own servers
Share with data brokers, in the worst case
Show up in Apple's privacy report in Xcode

Hide from store rules; stores add disclosure, manifest and ban rules

limits.reach_label: Everything the app can access, anytime
limits.differs: The same on both. Apple lists add on tools in a privacy report. Google shows data practices in the SDK Index.

story.what_it_is: Any code library inside an app can read what the app can read and send it to its own servers.

marketing.name: Third party SDK requirements
marketing.pitch: Apple requires privacy manifests and signatures for common SDKs so people can trust the data practices.

story.for_you: You never see these helper libraries. If you give an app your location, the ad or analytics code inside may use it too.
story.for_makers: Third party code inherits all of the app's permissions. A single SDK can collect location, IDs or contacts and pass them to a data broker, so the stores demand manifests, signatures and public lists.

use_cases.example: A free puzzle game includes six ad SDKs, each of which can read the device ID.
A weather app with a location grant also shares it with an ad SDK that sells it.
A login SDK sends your sign in details to the platform.
A crash tool sends device details to its own servers for debugging.
A data broker pays an app maker to add its SDK that collects location in the background.
Researchers inspect network traffic to find SDKs sending more data than declared.

story.android_note: Google Play lists SDK permissions in the SDK Index and requires disclosure in the Data safety form.
story.ios_note: Apple requires manifests and a short list of signed SDKs.

technical_bounds: No runtime isolation on either OS
Apple lists popular SDKs requiring signatures

abuse: Covert location or contact harvesting for resale

history.change: Google bans X-Mode (Outlogic) SDK from Play; Apple gave 14 days
Google Play SDK Index shows SDK data practices
Privacy manifest and SDK signature requirement
